title: Opponent plasticity in the direct and indirect pathways
excerpt: The two principal SPN classes are distinguished less by gross morphology alone than by their molecular markers, projection patterns, neuropeptide content, and–most critically for plasticity–the intracellular signaling cascades dopamine engages within them. Dir
html:
The two principal SPN classes are distinguished less by gross morphology alone than by their molecular markers, projection patterns, neuropeptide content, and–most critically for plasticity–the intracellular signaling cascades dopamine engages within them. Direct-pathway SPNs (dSPNs) express D1-type dopamine receptors along with substance P and dynorphin, and project monosynaptically to the basal-ganglia output nuclei (GPi/SNr), where their activation disinhibits thalamocortical targets and thereby promotes the expression of the selected action 1, 2. Indirect-pathway SPNs (iSPNs) express D2-type dopamine receptors along with enkephalin and adenosine A2a receptors, and project to the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe), initiating a polysynaptic cascade through GPe and STN that ultimately increases inhibitory output from GPi/SNr and thereby suppresses competing or undesired actions 1, 3. Two model architectures for striatal action selection (Figure). A computational test of pathway-specific plasticity predictions (Figure). The figure reports additional results from the cited study (Figure).

At the level of intracellular readout, opponent plasticity is implemented by opposite biochemical decoding of the same dopaminergic fluctuation. In dSPNs, dopamine increases bias recently eligible corticostriatal synapses toward potentiation through D1-dependent PKA signaling; in iSPNs, by contrast, decreases in dopamine relieve ongoing D2-mediated suppression and permit A2A-receptor- and CaMKII-dependent potentiation and spine enlargement 4. Thus a phasic dopamine burst and a phasic dopamine dip are not merely opposite motivational events broadcast to a passive striatum; they are interpreted by two distinct molecular substrates, such that positive deviations in dopamine preferentially reinforce direct-pathway representations, whereas negative deviations preferentially reinforce indirect-pathway representations 5, 6, 7. A 2026 review illustrates local dopamine–acetylcholine interactions (Figure) 18.

This opponent rule is no longer only an inference from slice physiology; key parts of it have now been observed in vivo. Real-time measurements of striatal signaling show that D1R- and D2R-expressing SPNs exhibit dichotomous, asynchronous PKA modulation during learning, with D1 populations preferentially tracking dopamine increases and D2 populations preferentially tracking dopamine decreases 6. In ventral striatum, Iino and colleagues further showed that appetitive conditioning initially generalizes through D1R-dependent mechanisms, and that subsequent discrimination learning is sharpened by brief dopamine dips–detectable on the order of hundreds of milliseconds–which disinhibit A2A-dependent spine enlargement in D2-SPNs 7. Opponent plasticity therefore appears well suited not only to strengthen rewarded actions, but also to refine overgeneralized policies by writing negative-outcome information into indirect-pathway ensembles 7. Dopamine release mode affects striatal projection-neuron excitability and spine density (Figure) 19.

A major recent advance is the recognition that the simple slogan "dSPNs learn from positive outcomes, iSPNs learn from negative outcomes" is, in its naive form, computationally inconsistent. In the standard model, dSPNs promoting the chosen action are potentiated when dopamine increases (positive RPE), and iSPNs suppressing unchosen actions are potentiated when dopamine decreases (negative RPE). The difficulty arises from the iSPN side: if iSPNs are active only when suppressing other actions (as in the classical model where active iSPNs suppress non-selected actions), then a dopamine pause after a bad outcome would strengthen iSPN synapses representing those other, non-chosen actions–actions that were not responsible for the negative outcome. This produces a pathological learning signal: the iSPN plasticity rule would reinforce patterns of suppression associated with negative outcomes rather than with the action that actually caused the bad result, effectively punishing the wrong actions 8. The resolution proposed by Lindsey et al. requires that functionally opponent dSPNs and iSPNs–that is, the dSPN promoting the chosen action and the iSPN also associated with the chosen action (which, when strengthened, would suppress it in the future)–are coactive during and immediately after action selection, so that both populations are eligible for credit assignment by the same dopamine transient. Under this arrangement, a dopamine burst after a good outcome potentiates the dSPN (via D1/LTP) and depresses the co-active iSPN synapse (via D2/eCB-LTD), both changes favoring repetition of the successful action; a dopamine pause after a bad outcome depresses the dSPN synapse and potentiates the co-active iSPN synapse, both changes favoring suppression of the failed action. The model’s central prediction–that functionally opponent dSPNs and iSPNs are simultaneously activated by efferent input following action selection–was confirmed in experimental recordings showing that direct and indirect pathway SPNs are broadly coactive during action initiation, consistent with the findings of Cui and colleagues who first demonstrated concurrent activation of both pathways during movement using fiber photometry 9, 8. The model further predicts that this coactivation structure enables multiplexing of action-selection signals and learning signals without interference, and facilitates off-policy learning in which the striatum can learn from actions driven by other neural circuits. A recent striatal model links dopamine-dependent plasticity and direct/indirect pathway activity to action selection and reinforcement learning (Figure).

The opponent plasticity architecture described above–D1-dependent potentiation after dopamine bursts, D2/A2A-dependent potentiation after dopamine pauses, and the coactivation structure ensuring both pathways are eligible for credit assignment by the same transient–has functional consequences that extend well beyond the reinforcement or punishment of individual actions, spanning distributional value coding, dissociable contributions to decision-making, cortical gating, exploration, and normative advantages in cost-benefit learning.

First, opponent plasticity provides a natural substrate for distributional reinforcement learning in the striatum. As discussed in the error-signal section, midbrain dopamine neurons encode a family of asymmetrically scaled prediction errors. Lowet and colleagues showed that D1- and D2-expressing SPNs complete this distributional code downstream by preferentially representing the right (optimistic) and left (pessimistic) tails of the learned reward distribution, respectively; chronic dopamine ablation disorganized these distributional representations without eliminating mean value coding, indicating that opponent plasticity is specifically required for distributional–rather than merely average–value learning 10. In their computational model, asymmetric plasticity rules operating on opponent SPN populations converge to expectile-like estimates, with D1 SPNs learning expectiles above the median and D2 SPNs below it, thereby harnessing pathway opponency for improved sensitivity to risk and outcome uncertainty 10.

Second, causal manipulations support dissociable pathway contributions to decision-making. Selective inactivation of D1R- versus D2R-expressing dorsal striatal neurons in mice revealed that D1R inactivation selectively impaired value-dependent action selection, whereas D2R inactivation selectively impaired value updating when contingencies changed 11. Optogenetic stimulation of the two pathways during visual and working-memory tasks further showed that direct-pathway activation increased contralateral responding and globally enhanced cortical activity–including the neural representation of a visual stimulus during a delay period–whereas indirect-pathway activation had the opposite effects, demonstrating that opponent plasticity reshapes not only striatal action probabilities but also thalamocortical representations over which perceptual decisions and working-memory maintenance operate 12.

Third, opponent plasticity endows the indirect pathway with a specific role in exploration, flexibility, and policy revision. In the posterior dorsomedial striatum, direct-pathway neurons are critical for encoding goal-directed action-outcome associations, whereas indirect-pathway neurons are specifically required for updating those associations during reversal–optogenetic inhibition of iSPNs, but not dSPNs, impaired reversal learning while leaving initial acquisition intact 13. Complementarily, dorsomedial striatal indirect-pathway neurons monitor the unreliability of the current action policy: their late-onset activity following unrewarded suboptimal actions represents lowered policy valuation and a heightened bias to probe alternatives 14. Lee and Sabatini provided a circuit mechanism for how this suppression of a failed action can simultaneously generate an alternative: iSPN activation suppresses the ipsilateral superior colliculus while exciting the contralateral colliculus via inter-collicular competition, triggering an alternative motor program rather than mere behavioral arrest; inactivation of iSPNs impaired both suppression of devalued actions and exploratory switching 15. Their recent synthesis proposes that the indirect pathway is governed by a three-factor learning rule in which dopamine dips potentiate iSPN synapses representing the action that caused the negative outcome, enabling learned avoidance while simultaneously–through competitive downstream interactions–facilitating transition to alternative actions; the indirect pathway is thus not merely a "stop" channel but a multifaceted system for avoidance, exploration, and policy updating sculpted by opponent plasticity 16.

Finally, the OpAL* model of Jaskir and Frank formalizes these opponent dynamics as a dual actor-critic system and demonstrates that the architecture confers normative computational advantages, particularly in environments with sparse reward and large action spaces, where separate "benefit" and "cost" actors develop complementary specializations that resolve explore-exploit tradeoffs more efficiently than single-pathway RL 17. These advantages depend on both opponency and nonlinear three-factor Hebbian plasticity–the biological learning rule–and the model captures patterns of risky choice arising from dopamine manipulations across species, suggesting that risk sensitivity emerges naturally from opponent plasticity rather than from a separate risk-evaluation module 17.
